title: Protocol and Asset
premise: Emrys Montrose, a sleep-wrecked interpreter haunted by a diplomatic incident he can't fully remember, is approached by a stranger claiming he once did her a favor she intends to repay. The repayment drags him into extracting Ilse Varga, a cryptographer defecting from a hostile intelligence service—but Ilse may be bait in an operation designed to flush out the mole who caused the incident Emrys has forgotten. As the extraction unravels into betrayal, Emrys discovers his missing memory holds the key to identifying the true traitor inside the delegation. In the end, Emrys chooses to surrender his anonymity and testify, trading his invisibility for belonging—and for the truth that finally lets him sleep.
about_author: Tamsin Dravenmoor is a former conference interpreter who spent a decade working behind glass booths in cities whose names she still won't say aloud. She writes thrillers about people fluent in other people's secrets and illiterate in their own.

chapters.title: The Favor That Never Happened
chapters.summary: Emrys Montrose, running on four hours of broken sleep, interprets a fractious trade session and notices a woman watching him from the gallery. Afterward, Mara Quist introduces herself and insists he once saved her life in Vilnius—a favor he has no memory of. She says debts should be repaid with interest. POV: Emrys. Beat: unease dressed as flattery; the first crack in his carefully maintained invisibility.

chapters.title: Ninety-Six Nights
chapters.summary: Emrys catalogs his insomnia ritual: the incident at the Riga summit three months ago, the gap in his memory, the delegation's polite silence. His colleague Denzil warns him to stay away from Quist, calling her a fixer for people who don't exist. POV: Emrys. Beat: dread deepening—we learn how fragile his cover of normalcy really is.

chapters.title: Interest Owed
chapters.summary: Quist lays out the job: extract Ilse Varga, a cryptographer who wants out, using Emrys's interpreter credentials as cover during the Vienna round. He refuses. That night someone leaves a photograph on his door—himself in Riga, mid-incident, timestamped from an angle no civilian could occupy. POV: Emrys. Beat: refusal collapses into coercion; the trap closes gently.

chapters.title: The Delegation's Polite Machinery
chapters.summary: Inside the peace delegation, Emrys maps its power players: chairwoman Odile Ferrant, security chief Bram Kessler, and the quietly indispensable aide Piers Lanyon. Everyone performs harmony while hoarding leverage. Emrys realizes the talks are designed to fail—and that someone profits from the failure. POV: Emrys. Beat: cold clarity; the theme of corrupted power takes shape.

chapters.title: A Woman Who Speaks in Cipher
chapters.summary: First contact with Ilse Varga at a museum reception, conducted entirely through interpreted small talk carrying double meanings only Emrys catches. She tests him with a phrase from Riga—words he shouldn't recognize but does, viscerally. POV: Emrys. Beat: recognition without memory; his body remembers what his mind lost.

chapters.title: Kessler's Ledger
chapters.summary: Security chief Bram Kessler summons Emrys, not to threaten him but to recruit him as an informal ear—report anything odd. Emrys agrees, now playing both sides. Interleaved: a fragmentary flashback of Riga, a corridor, shouting in a language he can't place. POV: Emrys. Beat: complicity begins; the reader feels the noose of divided loyalty.

chapters.title: The Extraction Rehearsal
chapters.summary: Quist walks Emrys through the plan: swap Ilse into the interpreters' rotation during the closing plenary, move her through the service corridors, out via the river gate. Emrys spots a flaw—the timing assumes the plenary runs long, which requires someone to make it run long. POV: Emrys. Beat: competence and creeping suspicion; the plan is elegant because it was built by someone inside.

chapters.title: What Denzil Knows
chapters.summary: Denzil confronts Emrys with evidence that the Riga incident wasn't random: the interpreter booth's audio feed was doctored, and Emrys was the only witness positioned to see who did it. His missing memory isn't trauma—it's possibly chemical. POV: Emrys, with a Denzil-driven scene. Beat: horror reframed; forgetting was done to him, and someone needed him quiet.

chapters.title: Ilse's Price
chapters.summary: Ilse reveals what she's carrying: not codes but a ledger of payments routed through delegation accounts—the corruption engine behind the doomed talks. She'll trade it only for passage and protection, and she names her condition: Emrys must be the one who carries her out. POV: Ilse (first shift). Beat: stakes sharpened; Ilse is sharp, frightened, and possibly lying about something.

chapters.title: The Long Plenary
chapters.summary: Extraction day. Emrys works the booth as engineered delays stretch the session—his own voice weaponized, nuance stretched to buy minutes. The handoff in the corridor goes clean until the river gate, where a second team is waiting. POV: Emrys. Beat: adrenaline and dread; the plan works exactly because it was expected to.

chapters.title: Bait
chapters.summary: The second team takes Ilse; Emrys escapes by reflexes he didn't know he had. Quist goes dark. Emrys realizes the extraction was never meant to succeed—it was designed to expose him, to force whoever erased his memory to react. He is the asset, not the agent. POV: Emrys. Beat: betrayal and vertigo; the ground truth of chapters 1–9 inverts.

chapters.title: The Mole's Signature
chapters.summary: Denzil decodes part of Ilse's dead-drop backup: payments trace to a cutout inside the delegation itself. Three candidates emerge—Ferrant, Kessler, Lanyon. Meanwhile Kessler reports Emrys's escape attempt, making him officially a suspect. POV: alternating Emrys/Denzil. Beat: paranoia institutionalized; every ally is now also a suspect.

chapters.title: Riga, Remembered Wrong
chapters.summary: Under a doctor's supervision arranged by Quist—who resurfaces, unapologetic—Emrys undergoes memory recovery. Fragments return: the corridor, a voice giving instructions in accented English, and his own hands passing a document he now understands he was tricked into carrying. POV: Emrys. Beat: grief and rage; memory returns as wound, not comfort.

chapters.title: Quist's Confession
chapters.summary: Quist admits the truth: she works for a rival service that has hunted the mole for two years. The 'favor' was fiction; Emrys was selected because the mole knows his face and trusts his silence. But she swears Ilse is real and still alive—for now. POV: Quist. Beat: reluctant alliance rebuilt on honesty at last; trust as calculated risk.

chapters.title: Where They Keep Her
chapters.summary: Tracking Ilse's captors to a safehouse outside Bratislava, Emrys and Quist find it already burned—except for one thing left deliberately: Ilse's cipher notebook, opened to a page keyed to delegation account numbers. A message, or a lure. POV: Emrys. Beat: dread of being read like a text; the enemy anticipates them perfectly.

chapters.title: Lanyon's Kindness
chapters.summary: Back in Vienna, aide Piers Lanyon offers Emrys sanctuary, sympathy, and a way out—all of which fits, too neatly, the profile of the voice from the recovered memory. Emrys plays grateful while testing him with a false detail about Riga. Lanyon corrects the detail. POV: Emrys. Beat: icy triumph curdling into fear; confirmation means the hunter knows he's hunted.

chapters.title: The Ledger and the Leak
chapters.summary: Ilse surfaces alive, having turned her own captivity—she fed her captors a poisoned copy of the ledger. The real one, she tells Emrys, names not just the mole but the foreign service backing him. She'll give it up only publicly, at the summit's final session. POV: Ilse. Beat: agency reclaimed; the defector becomes the most dangerous person in the book.

chapters.title: Countdown in the Booth
chapters.summary: Forty-eight hours to the closing plenary. Kessler closes in on Emrys; Ferrant maneuvers to end the talks early, which would destroy Ilse's window. Denzil volunteers to run interference and pays for it—arrested on manufactured charges. POV: Emrys. Beat: allies falling, clock compressing; sacrifice raises the emotional cost of the climax.

chapters.title: Everything Interpreted
chapters.summary: Climax at the closing session. Ilse moves on the floor while Emrys, in the booth, uses the live interpretation channel to broadcast the ledger's contents—turning the delegates' own translation infrastructure into the leak. Lanyon tries to cut the feed; Kessler must choose a side, and chooses, belatedly, the law. POV: Emrys. Beat: the interpreter's weapon is language itself; power exposed in front of everyone.

chapters.title: The Corridor Again
chapters.summary: Lanyon corners Emrys in the same service corridor where Riga happened, completing the mirrored geography. He offers Emrys his old life back—invisibility, silence. Emrys refuses aloud, on the record, as Quist's team closes in. Lanyon's arrest is quiet, bureaucratic, devastating. POV: Emrys. Beat: the personal climax; refusing erasure as an act of selfhood.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Fallout: hearings, leaked transcripts, careers ending. Emrys testifies about Riga fully, naming what was done to his memory. Ferrant resigns; Denzil is released; Ilse disappears into a new life she chose. Quist offers Emrys work. He declines—then asks her to stay for coffee anyway. POV: Emrys. Beat: cost tallied honestly; victory without triumphalism.

chapters.title: Sleep
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Emrys interprets a small, honest arbitration in a provincial town—no stakes, no shadows. That night he sleeps through until morning for the first time in ninety-six nights plus all the ones since. Final image: a stranger's kindness returned, interest paid, the debt closed. POV: Emrys. Beat: resolution as restoration of self; belonging chosen over invisibility.
